Summary:

The novelty of this paper lies in the combination of a variety of tools and concepts, none of which individually are new. Moreover, the authors published work on MDFF fitting of EM maps. However, this new combination (MD-based fitting of EM maps, combined with replica exchange and gradual resolution increase) works very well in the test cases that are presented in this work. The radius of convergence is impressive.

The main application of this combined method is for cases where the initial model is very far from the EM map. However, in practice the applications of their method may be somewhat limited since either (a) the EM map is near atomic resolution (3.5 A or better) allowing ab initio tracing, or (b) the map is lower resolution in which case higher resolution structures of fragments are generally needed in order to have confidence in the final model. The new method is probably most useful in the resolution range 4-7 A where ab initio fitting to the maps is not possible and when high-resolution structures are available of all components, but these components undergo large conformational changes.

Along similar lines, the advantages of cMDFF/ReMDFF over 'direct' MDFF are clearly demonstrated for high-resolution, although it would be helpful to know if there are also advantages of using cMDFF/ReMDFF over direct MDFF at moderate resolutions (lower than 4 A resolution).

Essential revisions:

1) A common practice in the EM field is to perform refinements against half maps to judge the degree over-fitting. Assuming that the authors have access to the EM data for one of the test cases, such over-fitting test should be performed – as shown in DiMaio, et al. (2013) Protein Sci, 22, 865-868 or Amunts, et al. (2014) Science 343, 1485-1489.

2) It was unclear how well the protocols work at the second step – ensuring an accurate model that sufficiently describes the density at the side chain level. In the absence of figures demonstrating the fit of side chains to density (an omission that should be corrected), one of the reviewers compared the provided model coordinates (source data to Table 1) with the deposited structure of β-galactosidase (PDB accession code 3J7H). This revealed substantial problems with the model. There are a large number of Ramachandran outliers (~10%); more than 1% of non-prolines are in cis-configurations (less than 0.05% are expected); the backbone of the region around the galactoside binding site is incorrect, and many of the side chains are not in their correct density. The authors themselves note 'even if the backbone is correctly placed, the MD force fields […] are incapable of providing sidechain geometries consistent with the map'. This may represent a considerable limitation to using cMDFF/ReMDFF to refine atomic models against sub 5 Å EM maps. It would be helpful if the authors could demonstrate that cMDFF/ReMDFF is capable of refining good starting models without disrupting backbone and side chain geometries. This would more accurately reflect the starting model for many of the potential users of cMDFF/ReMDFF. For example, the deposited model for β-galactosidase should be refined with cMDFF and ReMDFF and not just direct MDFF. The manuscript should provide guidance on how to preserve side chain geometries and the prevent cis-peptide bond formation during refinement. This would improve the utility of cMDFF/ReMDFF as a method of fitting a well-refined structure to classes of different conformational states that can range from high to mid resolution – a good test case might be CorA (Matthies et al. 2016. Cell, 164(4):747-756). Further statistics should be provided to demonstrate the quality of the model after cMDFF/ReMDFF. For example, root-mean-square deviations for bond lengths and bond angles and Ramachandran statistics, which are typically minimal requirements when reporting the quality of structural models. 3) The authors propose per-residue root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) values as a way of specifying the precision of atom positions. These are shown to correlate with local map quality, suggesting they can be used for model-to-map validation. In many ways RMSF values appear to be analogous to atomic B factors. It would be helpful to see a side-by-side comparison of a protein structure colored by local resolution, atomic B factors and RMSF (an expansion of Figure 3). One would expect them to correlate in a way that EMRinger and local correlation coefficient do not (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). What are the advantages of RMSF over B factors, which are a more established measure? Do the authors actually recommend depositing ensembles?

4) It is unclear what advantages are to be gained by utilizing RMSF values to determine the B factor for sharpening the map (which involves multiple simulations) compared to Guinier analysis performed during the standard post-processing procedure when both provide the same, or similar, values (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). Could RMSF values be calculated for different parts of the model to generate locally sharpened maps that subsequently improve refinement (although one suspects that applying a mask during post-processing would result in a similar effect)?

5) There is no relation of the presented method with "phase extension" approaches in crystallography where phase experimental phase information is generally much less accurate than amplitude information, and phase extension method make use of the inherently higher accuracy of the amplitude information along with approaches such as solvent flattening of map averaging. The cMDFF and ReMDFF approaches do not actually improve the EM map, they just use filtered less rugged density maps for better convergence of the global conformational changes. Please avoid this analogy.

6) The title is a bit misleading, reading "Ensemble-based refinement…". One might expect an ensemble refinement method, which this is not. Similar with the expression "ensemble-based flexible fitting" (end of Discussion): the flexible fitting itself is not "ensemble-based". Ensemble-based here simply refers to the calculation of RMSF value from the trajectory.

7) Figure 5: The plot describes map sharpening. Sharpening implies applying a negative B-factor, therefore one expects negative B-factor values on the x-axis.

8) This sentence – "well within the structural uncertainty represented by the 3 Å resolution limit of the crystallographic data" –, in the Results, is a bit misleading, since it sounds as if the structural uncertainty for 3 Angstroms data is 3 Å, which is not the case but unfortunately a common misconception. The accuracy of atomic positions is usually considerably higher than the limiting resolution of a crystal. Please remove or reword this sentence.

9) The authors should discuss in more detail the limitations and potential applications of their method as suggested in the summary above.

10) Overall, the manuscript should be edited to remove repetition (cloud computing is described as being cost-effective four times in the paper) and inaccuracies. The Materials and methods section is almost indistinguishable in style from the Results section and could be shortened considerably, with some of the more insightful descriptions moved to the Results (for example the first paragraph of the subsection “Fluctuation Analysis”). Additionally, many of the reference choices seem unnecessary. For example, in the first paragraph of the Introduction, describing how cryo-EM has evolved, the authors cite papers on NMR methods for complexes over 20 kDa (Clore and Gronenborn), membrane proteins by XFEL (Neutze et al.) and ribosome structures at mid-resolution (the papers by Rawat et al.). It would be better to cite one of the recent reviews on cryo EM, for example 'Cheng, Y. 2015. Single-particle cryo-EM at Crystallographic resolution. Cell, 161(3):450-7.

11) All starting and refined models should be provided as supplementary data files.

results.result: Cryo-EM has evolved into an effective structure determination tool that overcomes major bottlenecks of X-ray crystallography, including crystal preparation and capturing molecules in unphysiological states, making it suitable for resolving large macromolecular complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Cheng 2015, Unger 2002, Neutze et al. 2015) and represent accepted knowledge in the field about the advantages of cryo-EM over traditional crystallography methods.

results.result: MDFF has been successful for low-resolution (7-25 Å) cryo-EM maps, but recent hardware advances have enabled routine high-resolution (<5 Å) maps that pose challenges to traditional structure determination methods, requiring precise modeling of near-atomic features including sidechain conformations.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C9 establish the historical context and current challenges, supported by multiple citations documenting MDFF applications, hardware advances, and the recognized challenges of high-resolution map interpretation (Trabuco et al. 2008, Li et al. 2013, DiMaio et al. 2015, Barad et al. 2015).

results.result: The authors present cascade MDFF (cMDFF) and resolution exchange MDFF (ReMDFF) methods that sequentially re-refine structures against progressively higher-resolution maps, achieving a radius of convergence of ~25 Å and providing validation criteria based on RMSF, with tools available on Amazon Web Services.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 describe the core methodological contributions of the manuscript, supported by experimental data from β-galactosidase and TRPV1 refinements demonstrating the stated radius of convergence and validation capabilities.

results.result: In proof-of-principle tests with carbon monoxide dehydrogenase, direct MDFF converged to 7 Å RMSD from target, while cMDFF and ReMDFF achieved 1.7 Å and 1.0 Å RMSD respectively, extending the radius of convergence to at least 7 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C16, C18 present experimental data from the proof-of-principle computation with clear quantitative results shown in Figure 1, demonstrating superior performance of the new methods over direct MDFF.

results.result: For β-galactosidase refinement, cMDFF and ReMDFF achieved RMSDs of 0.7 Å and 0.9 Å from the target (vs. 3.7 Å for direct MDFF), with superior EMRinger scores (3.16 and 3.45 vs. 1.91), iFSC values (5.22 Å and 4.66 Å vs. 2.74 Å), and GCC improvements (0.67 vs. 0.56).
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 present comprehensive quantitative validation metrics from Table 1 and supplementary figures, demonstrating clear superiority of cMDFF and ReMDFF over direct MDFF across multiple quality measures.

results.result: For TRPV1 refinement starting from a model 25 Å deviated from target, cMDFF and ReMDFF achieved RMSDs of 2.4 Å and 2.5 Å (vs. 7.9 Å for direct MDFF), demonstrating a radius of convergence as high as 25 Å.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28 present experimental data from TRPV1 refinement demonstrating the methods can handle extremely poor starting models, with the 25 Å radius of convergence representing a major advance over existing methods.

results.result: ReMDFF exhibited faster convergence than cMDFF, reaching steady state in 0.1 ns vs. 0.8 ns for β-galactosidase and 0.02 ns vs. 0.27 ns for TRPV1.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 present experimental timing data comparing the efficiency of the two methods, with clear quantitative results supporting ReMDFF's superior convergence speed.

results.result: RMSF values during MDFF simulations correlate closely with overall and local resolution of EM maps, with lower resolution maps producing higher RMSF, and RMSF during MDFF correlating linearly with RMSF during unbiased MD simulations, reflecting the inherent flexibility of the macromolecule.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C35 present a novel validation approach supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing linear correlations between RMSF and resolution across multiple test systems (β-galactosidase, TRPV1, γ-secretase, proteasome), with the physical basis established through correlation with unbiased MD.

results.result: The B-factor corresponding to minimum RMSF coincides with that determined by Guinier analysis for optimal map contrast across multiple systems (β-galactosidase, TRPV1, γ-secretase), establishing RMSF analysis as an alternative method for B-factor determination that prevents over-sharpening while maintaining correlation with inherent dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37, C72-C78 present experimental data from Figure 5 and supplements showing agreement between RMSF-based and Guinier analysis-based B-factor determination across three systems, with EMRinger scores confirming optimal sharpening at minimum RMSF.

results.result: cMDFF and ReMDFF improve clash scores and rotamer geometries while incurring small costs in Ramachandran statistics, with refined model quality depending on search model secondary structure quality. Search models deviating 7-25 Å from target with ~3% Ramachandran outliers and 11-38% poor rotamers can be accurately refined, with moderate- to high-confidence homology models recommended as optimal starting points.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C60 present detailed structural quality analysis from Table 2 and supplementary data, demonstrating the relationship between initial model quality and refined structure quality, with practical recommendations supported by experimental results and citations to prior successful applications.

results.result: Fitting Cβ atoms to density is crucial for accurate sidechain placement, MDFF backbone placement does not guarantee correct sidechain geometries even with CHARMM36 force fields, and the cMDFF-fitted β-galactosidase model with per-residue fluctuations <1 Å represents an excellent representation of the thermodynamic ensemble.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 present findings from additional simulations (Appendix 1 - Section 7) with experimental data in supplementary figures, confirming limitations of force fields and establishing the ensemble-representative nature of fitted structures through low RMSF values.

results.result: RMSF, together with GCC, LCC, EMRinger, and iFSC, provides a comprehensive set of validation criteria for model and map quality, with RMSF's added value particularly evident at the local level where it resolves quality even with as few as 100 atoms, unlike EMRinger which does not correlate with local resolution for small residue groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 present a comparative analysis of validation metrics supported by experimental data in Figure 4 supplements, demonstrating RMSF's advantages over existing metrics for local quality assessment.

results.result: ReMDFF on Amazon Web Services converges to the target structure for carbon monoxide dehydrogenase in approximately 0.1 ns simulation time, requiring little wall clock time and incurring small monetary cost to users.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C92 present experimental data from cloud computing implementation in Table 3, demonstrating feasibility and cost-effectiveness of the approach on AWS infrastructure.

results.result: cMDFF and ReMDFF offer accurate fitting of atomic-level structures within sub-5 Å EM maps previously inaccessible to direct MDFF, with a radius of convergence at least twice that of Rosetta refinements, and ReMDFF's quick convergence makes it amenable to cloud computing applications.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 present summary conclusions supported by the comprehensive experimental data throughout the manuscript, with comparison to Rosetta supported by citation to DiMaio et al. 2015 and cloud computing feasibility demonstrated experimentally.

results.result: At high resolutions, the MDFF potential features multiple proximal local minima corresponding to recurring structural patterns, with energy barriers typically twice as high as in low-resolution maps, exposing MDFF to entrapment in local minima and causing direct MDFF to yield structurally poor models with high-resolution maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 present the theoretical basis for the methodological development, supported by experimental data in Figure 1 showing energy barriers and Figure 2 supplement 1 showing poor direct MDFF results, with citation to DiMaio et al. 2015 confirming the recognized problem.

results.result: cMDFF fits structures to maps of gradually increasing resolution with the smoothest map featuring a clear global minimum, allowing greater conformational exploration than direct MDFF. ReMDFF runs multiple replicas in parallel with advantages in efficiency and automation, and both methods outperform direct MDFF in quality and speed.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C54 describe the methodological design of cMDFF and ReMDFF, with the theoretical basis illustrated in Figure 1 and superior performance demonstrated by comprehensive experimental data throughout the Results section.

results.result: Equilibrium MD simulations of a single structure at room temperature typically exhibit RMSD values of about 3 Å relative to the initial or average structure, as confirmed for β-galactosidase.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 presents established knowledge about MD simulations supported by data shown in Figure 2 supplement 6, providing important context for interpreting the RMSD values achieved by the refinement methods.

results.result: Conformational flexibility causes heterogeneity in cryo-EM data producing lower local resolutions, B-factor sharpening is crucial for map interpretation, MD provides higher B-factors for poorly resolved regions that better represent conformational diversity, and most high-resolution cryo-EM maps have resolutions between 3-5 Å where traditional B-factor methods have limitations.
results.evaluation: Claims C66, C71, C81-C84 present established knowledge about cryo-EM and B-factors supported by multiple citations (Leschziner and Nogales 2007, Kuzmanic et al. 2014, Fernández et al. 2008, Rosenthal and Henderson 2003), providing context for the B-factor determination methodology.

results.result: In the 3-5 Å resolution range, B-factors could be estimated from MDFF and used to improve model building and refinement, with MDFF-derived values serving as initial estimates for resolutions better than 3 Å. A resolution-dependent weighting scheme combining different B-factor values could improve accuracy of atomic models from high-resolution cryo-EM maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 propose future applications and developments based on the findings but lack experimental validation of these specific applications. While the underlying RMSF-B-factor relationship is demonstrated, the proposed uses require additional work to validate.

results.result: ReMDFF provides an efficient automated method converging faster than direct or cMDFF, and cloud computing offers solutions to hardware access bottlenecks while allowing bundling of different software packages for standardized workflows.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 combine experimental efficiency data (Figure 2 supplement 3) with general statements about cloud computing benefits, with the practical implementation demonstrated through the AWS deployment.

results.result: Sub-5 Å EM maps can resolve proteins in multiple conformations, and MDFF provides a natural method to model flexible regions by fitting de novo models from one conformational state into density of other states.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 presents established knowledge supported by citation to Matthies et al. 2016. Claim C44 proposes an application of MDFF based on demonstrated capabilities, though this specific application is not experimentally validated in the manuscript.

results.result: Flexible fitting methods have facilitated structure determination from low-resolution EM maps for over a decade, with MDFF being a front-runner that has enabled discovery of complicated structures in modern structural biology.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 present established knowledge about the history and impact of flexible fitting methods and MDFF, supported by extensive citations documenting applications and developments in the field.
